title: Nowhere and everywhere
hookLine: reading too many authors scatters you: the one who is everywhere is nowhere

cards: Fourteen browser tabs. Three half-read books by the bed. Two podcasts paused in the middle.
A language app, a cooking channel, a course you paid for in January. None of it bad. All of it started.
Very little finished. Seneca's second letter praises Lucilius for not living like that, then warns how easily he could start. We met one line of this letter in year one, about reading slowly.
Today we go underneath it, to the restlessness itself.

teach.b: Seneca opens kindly. He's heard that Lucilius isn't rushing from place to place, and takes it as a sign of a settled mind. A mind in order, he says, can stop and spend time with itself.
Then the warning. Be careful that reading many authors and every kind of book doesn't make you as restless as constant travel.
In Gummere's translation, three words: Everywhere means nowhere. Seneca piles up pictures. A person who spends life traveling ends up with many acquaintances and no friends.
Food that comes straight back up doesn't nourish the body. A wound doesn't heal if you keep changing the medicine.
A plant moved again and again can't grow strong roots. Every picture says the same thing: depth needs staying.

teach.h: STAY WITH A FEW; DIGEST ONE.
teach.b: So stay with a few, Seneca says, and let them sink in. When you feel like a change, go back to someone you've already read. And each day take away one thought to digest.
Not because new things are bad.
But you can't take root in fourteen places at once. The restless person isn't everywhere. They're nowhere for very long.
The one who stays can finally arrive.

how: Readers following Seneca's advice sometimes stay with a few trusted authors, reread rather than skim, and take away one thought each day to carry.

firm beliefs that no argument can ever shake
a family history that goes back generations

s: Seneca opens the letter by scolding Lucilius
he opens kindly, praising a mind settled enough to stay in one place.
Seneca compares restless reading to constant travel
both leave you with many acquaintances and no friends.
Seneca says food that comes straight back up still nourishes
his point: what doesn't stay can't nourish, in food or in reading.

games.q: you're Lucilius. you've just finished a book and you're itching for something brand new. what does Seneca suggest?
o: start three new authors at once.
go back to an author you've already read.
games.why: when you want a change, he says, return to the ones you've read before. depth comes from staying.

practice: Take one short thing to read, a line you love, a verse, today's line, and read it once at normal speed. Then read it again, slower, as if you'd never seen it, and notice one word you missed the first time.
Stay with that word, and let it put down one small root.

wordCard.voice: Strong roots, what a plant can't grow if it's moved again and again: Seneca's picture for a mind that stays with a few books instead of scattering. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the one who is everywhere is nowhere, from Seneca's second letter.

carryVoice: Your line: go deep. One thought a day, digested, is plenty. That's day four hundred thirty-three.
